images.caption: Figure 1:GameAnything: From Any Inspiration to Playable Game Worlds.GameAnything transforms diverse inspirations, including films, game trailers, real-world footage, images, and literature, into playable game extensions. Middle: illustrates the agentic construction pipeline alongside benchmark statistics and model performance. Bottom: showcases representative game extensions across diverse gaming environments.

Figure 2:Overview of GameAnything.Left:the multimodal reference pool.Top right:each task gives a coding agent an input package of multimodal references and instructions; the agent works in the original game’s project and modding interfaces to build or edit playable content.Bottom right:the agent development loop with iterative refinement, and supported games and systems.

Figure 3:Overview of GameAnything-Bench.The left panel shows the distribution of 205 tasks across Construction and Editing, task categories, and input modalities. The right panel illustrates the benchmark construction pipeline, where multimodal references undergo information extraction, model cross-review, and human validation to produce 125 Construction tasks. Validated Construction checkpoints further support 80 Editing tasks covering appearance, content and structure, and behavior and flow.

Table A4:Open-source target games.Game information, original-game screenshots, and two example extensions per game from development trials. Reference frames are shown above the corresponding in-game results. Task counts refer to Construction tasks.

Table A5:Commercial target games.Game information, original-game screenshots, and two example extensions per game from development trials. Reference frames are shown above the corresponding in-game results. Task counts refer to Construction tasks.

Table A10:Construction of an image-only task about minecart mechanics. Rubrics are abridged and image numbers match those shown to the agent. Wikimedia Commons credits are img01 by Flocci Nivis under CC BY 4.0, img02 by Ronald Werner under CC BY-SA 4.0, img03 by the Mining Museum of the Basque Country under CC BY-SA 4.0, img04 by Fernost in the public domain, and img05 by Timothy Titus under CC BY-SA 4.0.
Table A11:Construction of a video-only scene and world task from a film trailer. Rubrics are abridged, and timestamps refer to the source video.

Table A12:Hybrid video and image task construction for a scene and world objective. The video provides the ground-level experience, while separately collected images provide missing layout information. The top row shows clip frames and the lower row shows images. Rubric items are abridged, with a superscript x indicating cross-reference criteria. Studio concept art and theme-park photographs are used as private references.

Table A13:Editing task case study based on a video and text Construction task in Godot TPS. Three edits, one per class, share a validated checkpoint. The top row compares two reference frames with three checkpoint frames. Rubrics are abridged, and a superscript t marks trap items.

Table A14:Editing task case study based on a video, text, and image Construction task in Stardew Valley. Three edits, one per class, share a validated checkpoint. The top row pairs trailer frames with matching checkpoint scenes. Rubrics are abridged, and a superscript t marks trap items.

Table A15:Executability gate probes. Each probe runs the same inputs on the modified and an unmodified game under matched conditions and compares the outcomes; the thumbnail shows the function it checks.

Table A16:Structured runtime state returned by thegame statecall. Top: per-gameenginefields by kind; every game also returns content added by the modification in themodfield and on-screen text.†Read from adapter code only. Bottom: five evaluated submissions, each a replay screenshot with an excerpt of its paired snapshot.

Figure A3:The GameAnything web application forDream of the Red Chamberin Minecraft. The left panel lists projects and rounds, the center shows an agent conversation, and the right displays extracted scenes with source evidence, grounding status, and editable review controls. Project steps appear across the top.

Figure A4:Decision cards fromDream of the Red Chamberand a Hong Kong food project. Panels a to c show source understanding, design choices, and visual previews. Panel d shows permission controls. Panels e and f show project approval and the final result alongside the selected preview.

Figure A5:Workspace pages from the San Diego project in Cities: Skylines. Panel a shows a playtest video with chapters, time-anchored feedback, reference comparisons, and review controls. Panel b displays the development state and evidence. Panel c shows live development progress.

Table A32:Iterative development of Hogwarts in Minecraft across four versions and 21 critic rounds. Each column tracks the same location from the first round to the final version. The top row shows the agent’s interpretation of the source novel. User feedback is provided between versions, and quotations are translated.

Table A33:Iterative development of the Grand View Garden fromDream of the Red Chamberin Minecraft across six versions and 28 critic rounds. Columns track the main gate, Daguan archway, and Yihong moon gate. The final row uses the same viewpoints as the earlier critic shots. Amber borders mark user-annotated tour frames. The top row contains the public-domain source text. Quotations are translated.

Table A34:Iterative development of San Diego locations in Cities: Skylines across three phases and 12 critic playtests. Each row shows the harbor, La Jolla Cove, and UTC from matched camera views, with critic scores shown in the row headings. The top row contains user photos and selected Wikimedia Commons images licensed under CC BY-SA. Amber borders mark user-annotated tour frames. Quotations are translated.

Table A35:Continued iterative development of the San Diego coast in Cities: Skylines from TableA34. This table shows phases 2 and 3 after user feedback. Views remain matched, and amber borders mark user-annotated frames.
